notes.trap: If the array argument is NULL the result is NULL, not a one-element array. A NULL element, by contrast, is appended as a real null entry.
Only available from Spark 3.5.0. A NULL element is prepended as a real null entry and is not ignored, while a NULL array gives a NULL result.
When every element is null the result is an empty array, not NULL. Only top-level nulls are removed; nulls inside nested arrays or structs stay.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CAST(array_compact(array(CAST(NULL AS INT), CAST(NULL AS INT))) AS STRING)

notes.trap: NULL elements are not dropped. All nulls collapse into a single null entry, and first-occurrence order is kept.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CAST(array_distinct(array(1, NULL, NULL, 1)) AS STRING)

notes.trap: NULL is treated as an ordinary comparable value, unlike SQL `=` semantics, so a null present in both arrays appears in the result. The output follows the order of the first array and is de-duplicated.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CAST(array_intersect(array(1, NULL), array(NULL, 2)) AS STRING)

notes.trap: This is a set union, not concatenation: duplicates are removed even when they occur only within one input array. Use `concat(...)` to keep duplicates.

NaN counts as greater than every other double, so `array_min(...)` ignores it whenever a non-NaN value exists, while `array_max(...)` would return NaN. NULL elements are skipped rather than making the result NULL.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CAST(array_min(array(CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE), 1.0D, NULL)) AS STRING)
